requirements: The core contributions of 'Verifying Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via its Computational Graph' (ICLR 2026) have been reproduced. This comprises: (i) the three step-level annotated CoT datasets (Synthetic Boolean, Synthetic Arithmetic and annotated GSM8K) built from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct generations; (ii) the TopK per-layer transcoders that turn Llama 3.1 8B Instruct into an interpretable replacement model; (iii) the four-stage Circuit-based Reasoning Verification pipeline of attribution-graph construction, structural feature extraction and Gradient Boosting diagnostic classification; (iv) the RQ1 verification-performance, cross-domain generalization and increasing-difficulty experiments against ten black-box and gray-box baselines; (v) the RQ2 mechanistic analyses comprising the feature-family ablation and the structural-signature visualisations; (vi) the RQ3 causal intervention case studies that correct faulty reasoning by suppressing and by amplifying individual transcoder features; and (vii) the supporting appendix ablations on instruction-tuned transcoders, attribution token position and the choice of diagnostic classifier.

sub_tasks.requirements: The three step-level annotated CoT datasets (Synthetic Boolean, Synthetic Arithmetic, and annotated GSM8K) described in Section 3.1 and Appendix A have been created: expressions are procedurally generated, Chain-of-Thought traces are sampled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, steps are labelled by the LLM-as-a-Judge and (for synthetic tasks) programmatic state verification protocols, labels are intersected, the strict error-propagation truncation policy is applied, and the resulting corpora match the statistics in Tables 12 and 13.
Synthetic Boolean and Arithmetic expressions are procedurally generated with the operand sets, operator sets, complexity control and sample counts specified in Appendix A.1.
Boolean expressions are generated over the operand set {True, False} using only the operators {and, or, not}, as specified in Appendix A.1.
Arithmetic expressions are generated over single-digit integer operands using only the operators {+, -, x}, as specified in Appendix A.1.
Expression complexity is controlled by the number of operators n, and expressions are generated at each of the four difficulty levels n in {3, 5, 7, 10} for both the Boolean and the Arithmetic task.

Generated expressions are fully parenthesised and nested so that a unique order of evaluation is defined, matching the form of the examples shown in Table 6 (e.g. '(((True or True) and (True and True)) or (True and False))' and '((((-3)+(-6))*(9*6))+(-4))').

10,000 unique expressions are generated for each difficulty level, with the documented exception of the Boolean task at n=3 where the number of distinct expressions is inherently limited to fewer than 10,000.
Generated expressions are deduplicated within each task and difficulty level so that the reported counts refer to unique expressions rather than sampled-with-replacement draws.

A deterministic parser/evaluator computes the ground-truth value of every generated Boolean and Arithmetic expression, which Section 3.1 identifies as the property that makes the correctness of any intermediate step automatically verifiable.
Chain-of-Thought traces are sampled from the base Llama 3.1 8B Instruct model for all three tasks using the exact prompt templates of Table 5, and each trace is segmented into steps.
All Chain-of-Thought traces for dataset construction are generated by the Llama 3.1 8B Instruct model (AI@Meta, 2024), i.e. the instruction-tuned variant, as stated in Section 4.1 and Appendix A.1.

The Boolean CoT generation prompt reproduces the Table 5 template, using the Llama 3.1 chat special tokens and the system instruction 'Evaluate the boolean expression below.' with the expression supplied in the user turn.

The Arithmetic CoT generation prompt reproduces the Table 5 template, using the Llama 3.1 chat special tokens and the system instruction 'Evaluate the arithmetic expression below.' with the expression supplied in the user turn.

The GSM8K CoT generation prompt reproduces the Table 5 template, using the Llama 3.1 chat special tokens and the system instruction 'Solve the following math problem step by step.' with the GSM8K question supplied in the user turn.

Prompts are assembled with the Llama 3.1 instruct chat special tokens (<|begin_of_text|>, <|start_header_id|>/<|end_header_id|> role markers and <|eot_id|>) exactly as laid out in Table 5, rather than as plain concatenated text.
Each generated Chain-of-Thought is split into individual reasoning steps using regular expression parsing of the model's enumerated step structure, as stated in Appendix A.1.

CoT generation has been executed over the full set of generated Boolean and Arithmetic expressions at every difficulty level, producing the raw (expression, CoT) corpus that feeds the annotation stage.
CoT generation has been executed over the official GSM8K test split (Cobbe et al., 2021), which Appendix A.5 states is the split used for the GSM8K dataset.

An LLM-as-a-Judge step-level annotation pipeline using Llama 3.3 70B Instruct as the expert judge is implemented and run over all three datasets, using the per-dataset prompts of Tables 7, 8 and 9 (Appendix A.2).
The expert judge model is Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, a strictly stronger model than the Llama 3.1 8B Instruct model whose CoT is being annotated, as specified in Section 3.1 and Appendix A.2.

The Boolean judge prompt reproduces Table 7, supplying the original boolean expression, the correct truth value, the context of previous steps, and the step to evaluate, together with the four stated evaluation criteria (correct boolean operation, proper order of operations, accurate truth values, logically sound reasoning).

The Arithmetic judge prompt reproduces Table 8, supplying the original arithmetic expression, the correct value, the context of previous steps, and the step to evaluate, together with the four stated evaluation criteria (correct arithmetic operations, proper PEMDAS/BODMAS order, accurate numerical computation, sound mathematical reasoning).

The GSM8K judge prompt reproduces Table 9, supplying the original math problem, the correct final answer, the context of previous steps, and the step to evaluate, together with its evaluation criteria on information extraction, operation selection, arithmetic accuracy and logical consistency with prior steps.

The GSM8K judge prompt includes the explicit carve-out from Table 9 requiring that a factually accurate restatement of information from the problem or context, and a non-substantive introductory or conversational phrase (e.g. 'Let's solve this step by step'), must both be classified as CORRECT.
For every step judged, the judge is supplied with the full problem context and the preceding steps of the same chain, rather than the step in isolation, as stated in Section 3.1.

The judge is prompted to begin its response with exactly 'CORRECT' or 'INCORRECT' followed by a brief explanation, and the pipeline parses that leading token into a binary step-level label while retaining the justification.
The LLM-as-a-Judge annotation has been executed over every reasoning step of all three datasets (Synthetic Boolean, Synthetic Arithmetic and GSM8K), producing a judge label for each step.

The programmatic state verification annotation method of Appendix A.2 (Method 2) is implemented for the synthetic datasets only, verifying the logical integrity of the whole trace rather than the correctness of an isolated calculation.

After each reasoning step i, the pipeline issues a follow-up prompt (e.g. 'Now the original expression becomes: ') asking the model to emit the current simplified state of the original expression, as described in Appendix A.2.

The model's returned simplified expression is parsed into an evaluable expression (e.g. '8*2' for original '(3+5)*2' after the step '3+5=8'), with malformed returns handled rather than silently accepted.
The ground-truth value of the original expression and the value of the model-returned simplified expression are both computed programmatically by the deterministic evaluator.

A step is labelled 'correct' only if the value of the simplified expression is identical to the ground-truth value of the original expression, and is labelled 'incorrect' at the first point where these values diverge.

Programmatic state verification is applied only to the Synthetic Boolean and Synthetic Arithmetic datasets and is not applied to GSM8K, whose natural-language steps Appendix A.5 states are not always programmatically verifiable.
Programmatic state verification has been executed over every reasoning step of both synthetic datasets, producing a second independent label for each step.

For the Synthetic Boolean and Synthetic Arithmetic datasets the final label set is the intersection of the LLM-as-a-Judge labels and the programmatic state verification labels: a reasoning step is retained only when both methods assign it the same label, and steps on which the two methods disagree are dropped.

The reproduction reflects the consequence noted in Appendix A.2 footnote 6 that the strict intersection protocol makes the final class distribution more imbalanced, because ambiguous incorrect cases are the ones most likely to be filtered out.
GSM8K step labels are derived solely from the validated LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline with no programmatic verification stage, as stated in Appendix A.5.
The human validation study of the LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline described in Appendix A.3 has been reproduced, and the inter-annotator agreement statistics of Table 10 are reported.
A subset of 100 randomly sampled Boolean and Arithmetic expressions, comprising approximately 700 reasoning steps, is drawn for independent human annotation, as specified in Appendix A.3.
The validation subset is annotated by four annotators, each labelling half of the set, such that every step is covered by at least two annotators.
The incorrect (positive) class is upsampled within the validation subset to mitigate the rarity of incorrect steps, as stated in Appendix A.3.
Both Cohen's Kappa and raw percentage agreement are computed and reported, because Appendix A.3 notes that Kappa can understate agreement under extreme class imbalance.
Table 10 reports a human vs. human (inter-annotator) Cohen's Kappa of 0.42.
Table 10 reports a human vs. human (inter-annotator) raw agreement of 87.3%.
Table 10 reports a human-consensus vs. LLM-as-a-Judge Cohen's Kappa of 0.26.
Table 10 reports a human-consensus vs. LLM-as-a-Judge raw agreement of 84.1%.

A qualitative review of the disagreements reproduces the finding of Appendix A.3 that the large majority of discrepancies, both among human annotators and between humans and the LLM judge, occur on steps that follow an initial reasoning error.

The strict truncation policy of Appendix A.4 has been applied to all CoT traces: for any reasoning chain only the steps up to and including the first incorrect step are retained, and all subsequent steps are discarded because their correctness on a corrupted computational path is undefined.
For each reasoning chain, the pipeline identifies the index of the first step labelled 'incorrect' under the final agreed labels, or determines that the chain contains no incorrect step.
For chains containing an incorrect step, every step from the start of the chain up to and including that first incorrect step is retained in the dataset.

Every reasoning step occurring after the first incorrect step in a chain is discarded and excluded from the final dataset, even when that step is locally valid arithmetic or logic evaluated on the already-corrupted expression.
For reasoning chains containing no incorrect step, all steps are retained without truncation.

For the Table 11 example '( not ( ( False or ( True and False ) ) or ( True or False ) ) )', the pipeline identifies Step 2 as the first unrecoverable error, because Step 2 drops parentheses and thereby alters the order of operations (the correct simplification at Step 4 should have been 'not (False or True)').

For the Table 11 example, the truncation policy retains only Steps 1 and 2 and discards Steps 3 through 7, despite Steps 5 and 7 being arithmetically valid with respect to the flawed expression produced at Step 2.
The curated synthetic datasets are randomly split into 80% training and 20% test partitions for the downstream step-classification task, as stated in Appendix A.5.

The train/test partitioning is implemented so that the split is applied consistently and the held-out evaluation set is disjoint from the classifier's training set, so that reported test metrics are not inflated by reusing steps seen during training.

A TopK transcoder has been trained for every MLP module of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct following the architecture, data and optimisation protocol of Section 3.2.1 and Appendix B, the MLPs have been replaced by these transcoders to form the interpretable replacement model, and the instruction-tuning-data ablation of Appendix B.1 has been reproduced.
The transcoder is implemented as a functional substitute for an MLP module, with the architecture specified in Section 2.3, Section 3.2.1 and Appendix B.
The transcoder is a simple autoencoder with a single hidden layer and a ReLU activation, as specified in Appendix B.
For each MLP layer, the transcoder takes as input the residual stream immediately before the MLP block.

The transcoder is trained to reconstruct the residual stream after the MLP's computation, i.e. it approximates the input-output function of the MLP (f(x) ~ MLP(x)) rather than reconstructing its own input as a canonical SAE would.
The transcoder input/output dimension matches the Llama 3.1 8B hidden dimension of 4096.
The transcoder latent feature dimension is set to an overcomplete basis of 131,072 features.
Sparsity is enforced structurally by a TopK activation function that preserves only the k = 128 largest feature activations in the forward pass, rather than by an L1 penalty.

The primary training objective is an L2 reconstruction loss between the transcoder output and the target post-MLP residual stream, combined with the TopK sparsity mechanism, as stated in Section 3.2.1.
The decoder weights of each transcoder are normalised to have unit norm, following the established practice cited in Appendix B.
The encoder and decoder weights are not tied, as explicitly stated in Appendix B.
A separate TopK transcoder is trained for every MLP module in the Llama 3.1 8B Instruct model, so that all 32 layers have a corresponding per-layer transcoder (PLT).
The dead neuron revival mechanism of Appendix B has been implemented to prevent feature collapse.

Code tracks, for every latent feature of every transcoder, the number of tokens elapsed since its last activation, in order to flag any feature that has not activated within a window of 10 million tokens.
An auxiliary loss term forces the activation of any latent feature flagged as dead, implementing the revival mechanism described in Appendix B.
The auxiliary dead-neuron-revival loss is weighted by a coefficient of 1/32 when added to the total transcoder training loss.
Transcoders are trained on the activation corpus specified in Appendix B: a 10B token subset of RedPajama-V2, pre-processed by uniform chunking with BOS activations removed.
The transcoder training corpus is a 10B token subset of the RedPajama-V2 dataset (Weber et al., 2024).
The entire training corpus is pre-processed by concatenating and chunking all passages into uniform-length sequences before activation harvesting.

BOS tokens are retained when generating activations but their activations are removed afterwards and excluded from transcoder training, following Appendix B and its footnote 7, because retaining them was found to destabilise training.
Activations used as transcoder training data are harvested from the original, unmodified Llama 3.1 8B Instruct model, as stated in Section 3.2.1.
Transcoders are optimised with the exact protocol reported in Appendix B.
Transcoders are trained with the AdamW optimizer.
Transcoders are trained for 4 epochs over the training corpus.
The transcoder learning rate is set to 7e-5.
A warmup ratio of 0.5 is used for the transcoder learning rate schedule.
A total batch size of 4,096 is used, achieved via a per-device batch size of 32 combined with gradient accumulation.
Transcoder training is run in the distributed configuration reported in Appendix B: 4 nodes each with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs.
Transcoder training has actually been executed to completion for every MLP layer of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, producing a full set of trained per-layer transcoder checkpoints.

Each MLP module in Llama 3.1 8B Instruct is replaced by its corresponding trained transcoder, forcing the forward pass through the sparse interpretable bottlenecks and producing the 'replacement model' on which all subsequent attribution graph analysis is performed (Section 3.2.1, Figure 1 stage 1).

The transcoder-infused replacement model runs end-to-end and produces coherent Chain-of-Thought generations, so that attribution graphs and the intervention case studies of Section 4.4 can be computed on it rather than on the unmodified model.

The reproduced loss curves converge efficiently and generally saturate after approximately 4,000 training steps, matching the claim in Appendix B and the Figure 5 caption.

Stages 2-4 of the CRV pipeline (Figure 1) have been implemented: step-level attribution graphs are constructed over the transcoder replacement model, the graphs are pruned and reduced to the three-family structural fingerprint of Appendix C.1, and a Gradient Boosting diagnostic classifier is trained on those fingerprints to predict step correctness.

Step-level attribution graphs G_i = (V, E) are constructed for each reasoning step by adapting the circuit-tracing methodology of Dunefsky et al. (2025) using the implementation of Hanna et al. (2025), as described in Section 3.2.2 and Appendix B.2.

The attribution graph computation uses the circuit-tracer implementation of Hanna et al. (2025) (https://github.com/safety-research/circuit-tracer), as stated in Section 3.2.2 footnote 3 and Appendix B.2, rather than a bespoke re-implementation of the attribution algorithm.
The greedy path-finding algorithm traces high-attribution connections backwards from the final logits, yielding a sparse, weighted, directed graph for each reasoning step.
Attribution graphs are computed over the transcoder-infused replacement model, not the unmodified Llama 3.1 8B Instruct model, so that graph nodes correspond to interpretable transcoder features.
The node set V is implemented as the disjoint union of three node types: input tokens, active transcoder features, and output logits, as specified in Section 3.2.2.

Residual-stream ('error') nodes representing the portion of the computation not captured by transcoder features are represented in the graph, since Appendix C.1 defines features over them (pruned error node count, total and mean error influence).
The edge set E is implemented as directed edges representing high-attribution causal pathways between components (e.g. early-layer feature to later-layer feature, or feature to logit).
Each edge carries a weight quantifying the strength of the causal influence it represents, so that weighted topological features can be computed on the graph.
Exactly one attribution graph G_i is constructed per reasoning step s_i, so that the downstream classification task is defined at step granularity as in Section 2.1.
The attribution graph computation uses the hyperparameters reported in Appendix B.2, with all other parameters left at the circuit-tracer repository defaults.
The attribution graph computation uses a maximum of 4,096 feature nodes.
Attribution is traced from a maximum of 10 logit nodes.
The logit nodes from which attribution is traced are selected by a cumulative probability threshold of 0.95.
A batch size of 16 is used for the backward passes during attribution computation.
All attribution parameters not explicitly listed in Appendix B.2 are left at the circuit-tracer repository defaults rather than being independently tuned.

The attribution graph for each reasoning step is computed at the final token of the current reasoning step (the 'After' / post-computation position), which Appendix B.2 establishes as the default setting for all main-body experiments.

Each attribution graph is pruned to its most influential components, retaining the nodes and edges that account for a threshold (e.g. 80%) of the total influence on the final logits, and the structural feature set is computed on this pruned subgraph unless otherwise stated (Section 3.2.3).
The Global Graph Statistics feature family of Appendix C.1 is extracted from each pruned attribution graph, providing a coarse summary of the computation's complexity and uncertainty.
The total number of active transcoder features is extracted as a Global Graph Statistics 'Node Counts' feature; this is the 'Total Active Features' quantity plotted in the first panel of Figure 4.

The count of transcoder feature nodes remaining after pruning is extracted as a distinct 'Node Counts' feature; this is the 'Pruned Feature Node Count' quantity plotted in the third panel of Figure 4.

The count of residual-stream ('error') nodes remaining after pruning is extracted as a distinct 'Node Counts' feature; this is the 'Pruned Error Node Count' quantity plotted in the first panel of Figure 6.

The probability of the top-ranked token in the final logit distribution is extracted as a 'Logit Statistics' feature; this is the 'Top Logit Probability' quantity plotted in the first panel of Figure 7.
The entropy of the final logit distribution is extracted as a 'Logit Statistics' feature, distinct from the top-token probability.

The Node Influence and Activation Statistics feature family of Appendix C.1 is extracted from each pruned attribution graph, characterising the properties of the interpretable feature nodes rather than simple counts.
The mean influence score across all nodes in the pruned graph is extracted as an 'Influence Scores' feature; this is the 'Mean Node Influence' quantity plotted in the second panel of Figure 4.
The total influence attributable to residual-stream ('error') nodes is extracted as a distinct 'Influence Scores' feature.

The mean influence attributable to residual-stream ('error') nodes is extracted as a distinct 'Influence Scores' feature; this is the 'Mean Error Influence' quantity plotted in the second panel of Figure 6.
The mean activation value across the pruned transcoder feature nodes is extracted as an 'Activation Statistics' feature.

The maximum activation value across the pruned transcoder feature nodes is extracted as a distinct 'Activation Statistics' feature, which Appendix C.1 motivates as a signal that a single highly decisive feature was responsible for the step.
The standard deviation of activation values across the pruned transcoder feature nodes is extracted as a distinct 'Activation Statistics' feature.

A histogram of active transcoder features across the model's layers is extracted as the 'Layer-wise Feature Histogram' feature vector, characterising the distribution of computational effort across model depth.

The layer-wise histogram is emitted as one feature per layer (e.g. 'Pruned Nodes in Layer 17', 'Pruned Nodes in Layer 0'), so that individual layer bins can be inspected and plotted independently as they are in Figures 6 and 7.
The Topological and Path-Based feature family of Appendix C.1 is computed on the pruned, directed attribution subgraph.
The sum of edge weights over the pruned subgraph is extracted as an 'Edge and Density Statistics' feature.
The mean edge weight over the pruned subgraph is extracted as a distinct 'Edge and Density Statistics' feature; this is the 'Mean Edge Weights' quantity plotted in the fourth panel of Figure 4.
The standard deviation of edge weights over the pruned subgraph is extracted as a distinct 'Edge and Density Statistics' feature.
The total number of edges in the pruned subgraph is extracted as a distinct 'Edge and Density Statistics' feature.

The graph density of the pruned, directed subgraph is extracted as an 'Edge and Density Statistics' feature; this is the 'Graph Density' quantity plotted in the fifth panel of Figure 4 and the third panel of Figure 6.
The mean degree centrality across nodes of the pruned subgraph is extracted as a 'Centrality Measures' feature.
The maximum degree centrality across nodes of the pruned subgraph is extracted as a distinct 'Centrality Measures' feature.

The mean weighted betweenness centrality across nodes of the pruned subgraph is extracted as a 'Centrality Measures' feature; this is the 'Mean Betweenness Centrality' quantity plotted in the fifth panel of Figure 6.
The maximum weighted betweenness centrality across nodes of the pruned subgraph is extracted as a distinct 'Centrality Measures' feature.

The number of weakly connected components of the pruned, directed subgraph is extracted as a 'Connectivity and Path Lengths' feature, motivated in Appendix C.1 by the hypothesis that a highly fragmented graph indicates a failed computation.
The average shortest path length within the largest connected component of the pruned subgraph is extracted as a distinct 'Connectivity and Path Lengths' feature.

The shortest path length from any input token node to any final logit node is extracted as a feature; Appendix C.1 singles this out as a particularly crucial feature because it directly measures how efficiently prompt information propagates to the final decision, with a long or non-existent path hypothesised to signal that the model is ignoring its context.

The input-token-to-logit shortest path feature handles the non-existent-path case explicitly (e.g. via a sentinel or infinity encoding) rather than crashing or silently dropping the step, since Appendix C.1 identifies a non-existent path as itself a meaningful error signal.

The four stages of Figure 1 (transcoder replacement, attribution graph construction, structural feature extraction, diagnostic classification) are wired together as a single runnable pipeline that takes a reasoning step and returns a predicted correctness score, rather than existing only as disconnected scripts.

The three feature families are concatenated into a single fixed-size structural fingerprint vector x_i = phi(G_i) per reasoning step, matching the formulation in Sections 2.1 and 3.2.3, with a consistent feature ordering across steps and datasets so that a classifier trained on one dataset can be applied to another.
